- If sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.7) in recent days, model tends to under-forecast; increase forecast by 1–2% to account for bullish momentum.  
- If sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.4), model tends to over-forecast; reduce forecast by 1–2% to reflect bearish pressure.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior day), model often overshoots in the next 3–5 days; apply a “cool-down” correction by reducing forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day for 3–5 days.  
- Model consistently underestimates true price in the first 5–7 days of a new trend; apply a “lag correction” by adding 0.5–1.5% to forecast for early days of upward trends.  
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (±0.2–0.4), model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a “reversion bias” rule: if price deviates >3% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast toward average by 0.5–1.0% per day.  
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to be overly conservative in the first 10 days; increase forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day for days 1–10 if sentiment is rising.  
- If sentiment is rising but price is flat or declining, model may overcorrect; reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% for 2–3 days to avoid “overbought” trap.
